references.text: The parallel account in Mark gives a detailed description of the evil spirit's effect on the boy – it throws him down, he foams at the mouth, gnashes his teeth, and becomes rigid. This corresponds with Luke's description that the spirit seizes him, he cries out, and the spirit convulses him with foam.

Mark describes how the spirit tore and mangled the boy when he was brought to Jesus – the spirit threw him into a seizure, and he rolled on the ground foaming at the mouth. The expression "σπαράσσει" (tears/mangles) is also used here.

Mark tells us that the spirit cried out, tore and mangled the boy violently, and came out, leaving the boy like dead. This shows the destructive and violent character of the spirit, as also described in Luke 9:39.

The parallel account in Matthew where the father describes his son's suffering – he is moonstruck and suffers greatly, often falling into fire and often into water. This is the same event as in Luke 9:39.

An unclean spirit that tears and mangles a person and cries out loudly before it comes out. The words "σπαράξαν" and "κράξαν" are used here in the same way as in Luke 9:39, showing the violent behavior of the evil spirit when it seizes someone.

The continuation of the same account where Jesus rebukes the unclean spirit, heals the boy, and gives him back to his father. The spirit threw the boy down and tore at him here as well, confirming the violent character described in verse 39.
A demon throws a person down among them before it comes out. This shows a similar pattern to Luke 9:39, where the spirit tears at the person and only reluctantly leaves him.

The description of the possessed man in the country of the Gerasenes who could not be tamed, who tore chains and shackles apart, and who constantly cried out and cut himself with stones. This illustrates the destructive and violent power of evil spirits, as also described in Luke 9:39.
